strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: representations learned via next-state prediction with temporally local contexts entangle static domain factors with transient dynamical cues, and simply increasing the temporal offset Δt is a simple, effective fix. The toy example in Appendix A makes the intuition concrete and verifiable.

The diffusion modification is technically well-developed: the representation-biased mixed-Gaussian prior (Eq. 9), the joint prediction target (Eq. 13), and the DDIM reverse step are derived coherently and grounded in existing structured diffusion work (Mixed DDIM), rather than presented as ad hoc engineering.

The experimental study is thorough for this problem area: four MuJoCo locomotion environments with morphological variations plus Adroit manipulation, IID and OOD settings, 5 random seeds, and multiple ablations covering Δt (Table 2 with linear probe/reconstruction metrics against a supervised upper bound), representation utilization variants (Table 4), guidance scale sensitivity (Table 7), and context-source variants (Table 8).

The generality of the lagged-context trick is validated beyond the authors' own method by injecting it into Meta-DT (Table 3) with consistent gains, which strengthens the claim that the contribution is the representation-learning technique rather than a bespoke pipeline.

Strong reproducibility: complete pseudocode (Algorithm 1), hyperparameter tables, dataset generation details, baseline implementation details, and a stated commitment to releasing code, datasets, and the data generation pipeline.
The limitations section honestly identifies the restriction to stationary dynamics and outlines future work on non-stationary settings.
weaknesses: Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos and grammatical errors throughout ('guassian', 'intead', 'condional', 'obeservation', 'explane', 'distangle', 'polices', 'contructed', 'impgility'), at least one incomplete sentence in Related Work ('such methods often rely on, yet fail to fully exploit...'), and informal phrasing in technical sections. While not fatal, the density of errors impedes reading and suggests insufficient polish.

The central claim of 'consistently superior performance' is overstated by the paper's own Table 1: DADP loses to Meta-DT on HalfCheetah OOD (3001 vs 3174) and to Prompt-DT on Door IID (1428 vs 2116), and all methods perform poorly on Relocate (DADP -5.81 vs expert -1.92), where gains over baselines are marginal. A more careful, hedged characterization is needed.

The theoretical justification is informal. The information-theoretic inequality I(ωt; z_{t-Δt}|...) ≤ I(ωt; τ_{t-Δt}|...) is stated loosely, the claim that z=(ξ,ωt) is a 'natural global minimum' of the prediction objective (Eq. 6) is heuristic, and identifiability of the static factor ξ is never formally established. The argument is plausible but not rigorous.

The OOD protocol is weak: 5 'unseen' domains are randomly sampled from the same factor space used to construct training domains, so OOD here means interpolation within the training parameter ranges rather than true out-of-distribution generalization. This weakens the generalization claims.

Some ablation results raise questions that are not adequately addressed: in Table 4, the Conditional Policy with Δt=1 performs far worse than the Null end-to-end baseline (2093 vs 3722 on Walker2d IID), and End-to-End Diffusion outperforms several representation-based variants, which partially undercuts the value of the learned representations; the mastery threshold of 60% expert performance is arbitrary and unvalidated.

The baseline set omits several methods discussed in the related work (e.g., Locoformer, CARoL, RMA-style approaches), limiting the strength of SOTA comparisons; the role of the guidance scale λ relative to the representation z is also under-explained given it appears prominently in the pseudocode.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem (zero-shot domain adaptation in offline control) and the proposed Lagged Context Dynamical Prediction is a simple, easy-to-implement idea with an intuitive motivation (breaking time-local cues in the context), supported by a clear toy example in Appendix A.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad: four MuJoCo locomotion environments with morphological variations plus an Adroit manipulation benchmark, with both IID and OOD protocols, and 5 random seeds with mean ± std reported.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough for this area: representation quality is measured with linear probe accuracy and parameter reconstruction across a sweep of Δt values (Table 2), the Δt modification is also validated on a different method (Meta-DT, Table 3), representation-utilization variants are decomposed step by step (Table 4), and guidance scale and context source are ablated in the appendix.

The paper claims to release a full open-source codebase, datasets, and data generation pipeline, which would aid reproducibility, and it honestly discusses its limitation to stationary (time-invariant) dynamics.
weaknesses: The headline claim that DADP 'outperform[s] or match[es] the best-performing baselines in nearly all cases' is overstated. In Table 1, DADP clearly loses on Door IID (1428 vs. Prompt-DT's 2116) and HalfCheetah OOD (3001 vs. Meta-DT's 3174), and several Adroit Relocate results differ by only ~0.03-0.3 with overlapping error bars (-5.81±0.15 vs. -6.06±0.40). No statistical significance testing is performed, and 'last checkpoint' evaluation is a questionable protocol.

The main empirical gains may be attributable to the diffusion-policy backbone rather than the proposed contributions: in the ablation (Table 4), the End-to-End Diffusion baseline (3722 IID / 2852 OOD on Walker2d) already beats Conditional Policy (2093/1617), Better Representation (3394/1813), and Mixed DDIM (3356/1908). Only the final 'w/ Predict' variant pushes above the null baseline, and it remains roughly on par with the Supervised-representation control (4014/2540), which weakens the claim that the unsupervised representation learning is the decisive ingredient.

Originality is modest on both components. The Δt/cross-episode context idea closely mirrors existing cross-prediction tricks in dynamics adaptation (e.g., CARoL, CaDM), and the diffusion-injection scheme is essentially a direct application of structured diffusion models with a shifted Gaussian prior (Mixed DDIM, Jia et al., 2024) plus a reparameterization of the prediction target. Notably, MetaDiffuser — explicitly identified as the closest work — is absent from the empirical baselines, so the claimed improvement over the closest prior diffusion-based method is not actually demonstrated.

The theoretical justification is informal and loose. The information-theoretic argument (I(ωt; z_{t−Δt}|st,at,ξ) ≤ I(ωt; τ_{t−Δt}|st,at,ξ)) is trivially true and does not establish disentanglement; the Δt→∞ analysis assumes zero prediction loss and an averaged-velocity optimum without proof. There is no formal guarantee that the representation retains ξ and discards ω.

The zero-shot setting is weaker than it sounds: contexts are collected online during the rollout (cold start), so the policy still needs in-domain interaction history before adaptation; the practical implications of this cold-start phase are only partially explored.

CORRO's catastrophically poor results (e.g., -867 on Ant IID) suggest possible under-tuning or misconfiguration of baselines, raising concerns about the fairness of comparisons; the paper does not report baseline hyperparameter search effort.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos and grammatical errors throughout ('polices', 'guassian', 'implicilty', 'condional', 'explane', 'obeservation', 'desing', 'implicilty', 'Pesudocodes'), inconsistent notation (states/actions vs. U, M masking appears only in pseudocode and is never explained in the main text), Figure 1 lacks axis labeling details, and the newly introduced 'mastery' metric uses an arbitrary 60% threshold under which even the best method reaches only 44% on Walker2d — a result presented as a strength but arguably modest in absolute terms.

The evaluation scope for manipulation is thin: only 3 domains from a pre-existing ODRL dataset, with the OOD 'Medium' split sandwiched between the Easy/Hard training domains, which does not stress-test generalization the way the locomotion morphological variations do.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete, well-motivated problem: learned domain representations from dynamical prediction entangle static domain factors with time-varying dynamical properties, which harms downstream policy conditioning. The Lagged Context Dynamical Prediction is a simple, plausible, and unsupervised remedy, supported by a clear toy example (Appendix A) that makes the mechanism intuitive.

The representation-injection design into the diffusion process (mixed-Gaussian prior via a structured DDIM formulation plus a reformulated joint prediction target) is technically sensible, clearly derived (Eqs. 9–14), and grounded in existing structured diffusion literature (Jia et al., 2024).

The empirical evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: four MuJoCo locomotion environments with morphological variations, an Adroit manipulation benchmark, three established baselines plus an end-to-end diffusion baseline, 5 random seeds with mean±std, and both IID and zero-shot OOD settings.

Ablations directly address the paper's three research questions: the effect of Δt on representation quality (Table 2, Figure 3), the effect of representation utilization (Table 4, Figure 4), and transferability of the lagged-context idea to another method (Meta-DT, Table 3), which is a nice generality check. Additional ablations on guidance scale and context source (Appendix C) further support robustness.
The authors promise release of code, datasets, and the data generation pipeline, and include hyperparameter details and pseudocode sufficient for reimplementation.
weaknesses: Writing quality is below the bar for a main-track submission. There are numerous typos and grammatical errors throughout ('polices', 'incoperates', 'implicilty', 'guassian', 'observatoin', 'desing', 'explane', 'intead', 'distangle', 'contructed'), and the main-text formulation is inconsistent with the pseudocode: Eq. (9)/(13) use (1−√ᾱt)z while Algorithm 1 uses αk(x0−λz)+λz with a guidance scale λ that never appears in the main text. Notation is also inconsistent (a^t vs x^t, z vs xT = z + ε).

The theoretical justification is informal. The information-theoretic argument (I(ωt; z_{t−Δt} | st, at, ξ) ≤ I(ωt; τ_{t−Δt} | st, at, ξ)) is a trivial data-processing inequality that does not establish that ξ is retained or that the representation converges to a static descriptor; the Δt→∞ limit argument is heuristic and the derived 'averaged varying properties' component is acknowledged but not analyzed. The claim of 'unsupervised disentanglement' is empirically supported by probes but theoretically loose.

There is a train/test mismatch that is under-discussed: the representation is trained with contexts from other episodes in the same domain (Δt→∞), but at zero-shot test time the context is online-collected recent history from the current episode. Appendix C.2 partially mitigates this concern empirically, but the main text does not acknowledge or analyze it.

The 'consistently superior performance' claim is overstated: DADP underperforms Meta-DT on HalfCheetah OOD (3001 vs 3174) and Prompt-DT on Door IID (1428 vs 2116), and the ablation itself notes End-to-End Diffusion outperforms several proposed variants. 'Outperforming or matching in nearly all cases' would be the accurate characterization.

Missing empirical comparison with the closest prior work: MetaDiffuser (Ni et al., 2023) is described in the related work as the closest method (also injecting learned representations into diffusion) but is never compared against empirically; the argument that its representations are entangled is asserted rather than tested.

Novelty is modest: the Δt/cross-episode context trick is a simple sampling change, and the prior-biasing mechanism directly adapts Mixed DDIM; the contribution is primarily an application-level combination, which limits significance even if execution is solid.
Some results are reported with large variances (e.g., Meta-DT on Ant OOD 3187±899), and the paper does not report significance tests, making some close comparisons hard to interpret.

strengths: The core idea — Lagged Context Dynamical Prediction (∆t → ∞) to disentangle static domain information from time-varying signals — is simple, well-motivated, and supported by an information-theoretic argument, a worked toy example (Appendix A), and direct diagnostics (linear probe accuracy, reconstruction loss, t-SNE, and within-domain std in Table 12).

The representation-utilization mechanism (representation-biased mixed Gaussian prior plus a joint noise/representation-shift prediction target, Eqs. 9–14) is a clean and technically careful adaptation of structured diffusion (Mixed DDIM) to domain-conditioned policies, with a complete derivation.

Empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for a paper of this scope: main benchmark across 6 environments with Seen/Unseen/OOD settings, 5 seeds, ∆t ablation across four MuJoCo environments (Table 2), utilization ablation (Table 3, extended to Ant/Hopper in Table 11), guidance-scale sensitivity, context-source variants, non-stationary dynamics, one-step inference efficiency, and a ∆t ablation applied to Meta-DT (Table 6) showing the idea transfers across architectures.
Reproducibility is strong: full hyperparameters, OOD parameter ranges, dataset generation details, pseudocode, and a stated open-source release of code and datasets.
The paper is honest about scope (stationary dynamics only, shared reward function), explains why Hopper's representations are intrinsically hard to separate, and discusses limitations candidly.
weaknesses: The closest related method, MetaDiffuser, is not compared empirically; the paper substitutes indirect ablations (different ∆t, conditional vs. prior injection). While understandable, this weakens the SOTA claim since the claimed core differences are validated only within the authors' own pipeline.

Benchmark results are mixed rather than uniformly dominant: Meta-DT beats DADP on HalfCheetah Unseen (3174 vs. 3001), Prompt-DT wins Door Seen (2116 vs. 1428), and DADP ties Meta-DT on Relocate. The narrative of 'consistently superior performance' overstates these cases.
The baseline set is narrow (CORRO, Prompt-DT, Meta-DT, one end-to-end diffusion); stronger recent sequence-modeling approaches (e.g., Locoformer, cited in related work) are not evaluated.

Some technical details are under-specified: the dimensional compatibility between the representation z (dim(s)+dim(a)) and the trajectory-space variable a^0/x0 in Eqs. 9–14 is not explained, and the role of the guidance scale λ appearing in the pseudocode but not in the main-text equations is unclear until Appendix C.2.

Hopper representation quality remains poor (26.4% probe accuracy vs. 99% supervised), showing the method's limitation when domain signals are weak in behavior data; the paper acknowledges but does not resolve this.
The 'mastery' metric (60% of expert threshold) is introduced ad hoc; sensitivity of conclusions to this threshold is not analyzed.
Presentation has numerous typos and grammatical issues (e.g., 'guassian', 'intead', 'implicilty', 'Appedix', 'observatoin', 'distangle') that, while minor, reduce polish.

strengths: The paper is well-organized with a clear problem statement: domain representation learning via dynamics prediction entangles static domain factors with transient, time-local information. The proposed remedy (Lagged Context Dynamical Prediction, Δt → ∞) is simple, parameter-free, and well-motivated by the toy example in Appendix A.

The experimental scope is broader than much prior work: four MuJoCo locomotion environments with morphological variations plus Adroit manipulation, with three evaluation regimes (Seen, Unseen, OOD) and clearly documented out-of-support parameter ranges (Appendix C.4).

The ablation program is unusually thorough: Δt sweeps (Table 2), utilization variants (Table 3, Table 11), within-domain std as a direct disentanglement diagnostic (Table 12), context-source ablations (Table 8), guidance-scale sensitivity (Table 7), non-stationary dynamics (Table 9), and one-step inference efficiency (Table 10).
The transfer of the Δt idea to Meta-DT (Appendix C.1) supports the claim that lagged context is a general representation-learning improvement, not tied to the diffusion pipeline.
Open-sourced codebase, datasets, and data-generation pipeline, with detailed hyperparameters and pseudocode, supports reproducibility.
The limitations section honestly identifies the stationary-dynamics restriction and the inability of the current design to retain time-varying information.
weaknesses: Overclaimed results relative to the evidence. The text states DADP 'outperform[s] or match[es] the best-performing baselines in nearly all cases,' but Table 1 shows meaningful losses: HalfCheetah Unseen (Meta-DT 3174 vs. DADP 3001), Door Seen (Prompt-DT 2116 vs. DADP 1428), and Door Unseen (Prompt-DT 1080 vs. DADP 1494 except Relocate). On manipulation the gains are modest or absent. Similarly, Table 11 contradicts the claim in Section 5.3.2 that 'DADP achieve[s] superior performance across all the variants': on Hopper, 'Better Representation' (1710) beats DADP (1643), and on Ant Unseen, Mixed DDIM (3527) beats DADP (3495).

No direct comparison with the closest prior work, MetaDiffuser. The implicit-ablation proxy (Δt = 1 vs. ∞; conditioning vs. prior injection) is reasonable given the code is unavailable, but it does not establish superiority over the actual method, and the overall novelty over MetaDiffuser is incremental: the two contributions are a temporal-lag heuristic and a prior-biasing scheme that explicitly builds on Mixed DDIM (Jia et al., 2024).

The theoretical justification is informal. The information-theoretic argument is a loose inequality, and the Δt → ∞ limit is admitted to yield z = (ξ, ω̄) — i.e., the representation still contains an averaged time-varying component rather than pure static domain information. Calling this 'disentanglement' overstates what is achieved; the Hopper results (probe accuracy 26.4% vs. supervised 99%) further show the mechanism fails when domains are behaviorally similar.

Internal tension in the narrative: Section 5.3.2 notes that 'End-to-End Diffusion outperforms many variants,' including representation-conditioned policies, which undercuts the paper's own motivation that entangled/conditional representations harm diffusion policies and weakens the significance of the proposed utilization scheme.

The 'mastery' metric is introduced without justification for the 60%-of-expert threshold, and it appears in Table 3 where several ablation cells are missing or inconsistent with Table 11 (e.g., the Conditional Policy with Δt = 1 scores 2093 on Walker2d Seen while Table 11-style configurations differ), making the ablation story harder to verify.

Writing quality is below the bar for the main track: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('implicilty,' 'guassian,' 'apative pooling,' 'intead,' 'desing,' 'condional,' 'introudce,' 'Pesudocodes,' 'observatoin'), a partially unreadable Figure 1, and loosely defined notation (e.g., the role of the guidance scale λ is unclear in Eq. (9) vs. Algorithm 1).

The representation learning requires sampling the context from another episode in the same domain, which implicitly assumes domain-labeled grouping of the offline data; the paper does not discuss how this pairing is constructed or how sensitive the method is to this assumption.

CORRO performs catastrophically (negative returns in nearly all settings), which raises concerns about baseline tuning fairness; the baselines omit recent strong sequence models (e.g., Locoformer) on the main benchmark.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly articulated: using a large temporal offset (∆t → ∞) between context and prediction target to filter out time-varying information from learned domain representations, supported by an information-theoretic argument (Sec. 4.1) and an explicit toy case (Appendix A).

The representation-quality evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: linear probe accuracy, parameter reconstruction loss, t-SNE visualizations (Fig. 3, 6), and a direct within-domain std diagnostic (Table 12) all consistently support the disentanglement claim.

The empirical evaluation is broad: four MuJoCo environments with morphological (not just friction) variations plus Adroit manipulation, with Seen/Unseen/OOD splits, 5 seeds, and clearly documented OOD parameter ranges (Appendix C.4).

Ablations isolate each design decision: ∆t effect on representation quality (Table 2), representation utilization variants (Table 3, 11), guidance scale sensitivity (Table 7), context source (Table 8), and the lagged-context trick is also validated on a different architecture (Meta-DT, Table 6), which strengthens generality of the representation-learning idea.

Practical auxiliary evaluations are valuable: non-stationary dynamics robustness (Table 9), one-step DDIM inference efficiency (Table 10), and open-sourced code, datasets, and data-generation pipeline with detailed hyperparameters (Tables 4, 5) support reproducibility.
The limitation discussion is honest and specific (stationary-dynamics assumption, inability to disentangle while retaining time-varying information), rather than perfunctory.
weaknesses: The theoretical treatment is informal. The key claims — that z_{t-∆t} converges to (ξ, ω̄) and that ∆t → ∞ is the universal optimum — are heuristics backed by an information inequality that is loose and not turned into a theorem or guarantee. The toy case assumes zero prediction loss, which is unrealistic.

The ∆t → ∞ implementation requires sampling the context from another episode in the same domain (Algorithm 1: 'Rebuild random domain-based paired index'), implicitly assuming domain identity labels for the offline data during training. This assumption is not discussed as a limitation, and its practicality in truly unlabeled settings is unclear.

No direct comparison with MetaDiffuser (the closest diffusion-based meta-RL method) is possible because it is not open-sourced; the implicit ablation-based comparison is a reasonable workaround but weakens the 'SOTA over prior methods' claim.

Several headline results are not as dominant as the text suggests: on HalfCheetah Unseen, Meta-DT outperforms DADP (3174 vs 3001); on Door Seen, Prompt-DT substantially outperforms DADP (2116 vs 1428); Door and Relocate gains over Meta-DT are marginal. The claim 'outperforming or matching the best-performing baselines in nearly all cases' deserves more careful qualification.

CORRO performs catastrophically (near-random scores), raising the possibility of under-tuned baselines rather than a fair comparison; the Meta-DT baseline is also modified (reward decoder removed), which could disadvantage it relative to its published results.

The representation-injection mechanism (mixed Gaussian prior, joint prediction target) is largely adapted from Mixed DDIM (Jia et al., 2024) and the diffusion-prior structure is borrowed; the novel technical contribution is mostly the lagged-context representation learning plus the application, which is a modest conceptual advance.
The 'mastery' metric is newly defined by the authors with an arbitrary 60% threshold and is used as a headline claim; its sensitivity to the threshold is not reported.

Writing quality needs attention: numerous typos and grammatical issues throughout ('impliciltly', 'guassian', 'intead', 'observatoin', 'distangle', 'apative pooling', 'desing', 'introudce'), which undermine polish for a main-track submission.

The encoder is frozen after stage-1 training; the interplay between representation staleness and the non-stationary dynamics results (which still work surprisingly well) deserves more analysis than the hypothesis offered in Appendix C.5.
